title: RCMP works to rebuild image in B.C.
article: Linda Bush knew her fight with the RCMP was over when they stopped treating her as a nuisance and began listening.

Five years ago her son Ian was shot dead by an officer at the RCMP detachment in the B.C. interior town of Houston. Ever since then, Bush has fought the RCMP over what she considered major mistakes made by the force.
She filed a civil suit hoping to get answers but late last month, Bush dropped the case.

"There's been new policies and most importantly, a change of attitude," said Bush in an interview. "For a long time, they treated me as if I was making a big fuss over nothing, that I was just a traumatized mother unable to deal with reality. Nobody speaks to me that way any more. Nobody belittles any of the things that are happening."

It's hard to imagine how much worse the RCMP's reputation could have been following the death of Ian Bush in 2005 and of Polish immigrant Robert Dziekanski in Oct. 2007. Dziekanski died after he was Tasered during an encounter with four Mounties at Vancouver International Airport. Officers complained about being verbally abused in coffee shops and taunted while they were in uniform by the public. Polls indicated public confidence in the RCMP was at near-record lows.
But over the last two months, the RCMP have announced a financial settlement to Dziekanski's mother and apologized and reconciled with Bush, appearing at a press conference with her.

"Your input to the ongoing refinement of RCMP policy and procedures has been significant," said Chief Superintendent Craig Callens in thanking Bush. "Your efforts have contributed to the improvements that have been made at the Houston Detachment since your son's death, as well as in other areas of the RCMP."

Simon Fraser University criminologist Rick Parent, a retired police officer, and an expert in police shootings, said for the last few years, the RCMP's biggest issue has been public opinion. Senior officials have had no choice but to address the public perception that officers were too quick to respond with force.

"When the police are involved in deaths, the public takes note of that," said Parent. Before the incidents, the force's approval rating in the province was over 80 per cent, he added. Since the two high-profile deaths, the RCMP's approval rating now hovers around 60 per cent on good days.

During the Vancouver Olympics, the RCMP was generally praised for the way it led a force of 10,000 police officers from around the country and that helped begin the process of improving the force's reputation, according to Parent.
Former RCMP complaints commissioner Paul Kennedy said the deaths of Bush and Dziekanski, whose final moments were captured on video, damaged the RCMP's reputation.

The incidents highlighted two major issues that the RCMP were unprepared to deal with, said Kennedy whose office was an independent watchdog for the force. Last year, the government opted not to renew Kennedy's term.

In the Bush case, the RCMP investigated its own officer. The force questioned the lone officer on duty, Constable Paul Koester, then concluded the member acted in self-defence. No charges were laid. Kennedy said he also understands the public's outrage at the RCMP's use of the Taser gun on Dziekanski, especially the rapid deployment of the weapon, within 30 seconds of the officers' encounter with the immigrant.

"The public sees the obvious issues in the RCMP investigating itself," said Kennedy. "The RCMP in the Dziekanski case has been an object lesson for all police forces that they need to have strong policies and parameters in place when it comes to Tasers."
Walter Kosteckyj, a former RCMP officer and lawyer for Zofia Cisowski, Dziekanski's mother, said he's satisfied that public outrage and the loss of public confidence led the RCMP to make changes.

"There is now an acknowledgment that they can't be investigating themselves and they need to train their officers better in what's appropriate use of force," said Kosteckyj. "They've apologized but most importantly, they've recognized what they've done wrong."
